entry.reasons: The entry accurately reflects the essential knowledge statements 3.1.A.2 and 3.1.A.3 from the AP Physics 1 CED, which state that translational kinetic energy is a scalar quantity and that different observers may measure different values depending on their frame of reference.

Topic 3.1 states, “Translational kinetic energy is a scalar quantity” (3.1.A.2) and “Different observers may measure different values of the translational kinetic energy of an object, depending on the observer’s frame of reference” (3.1.A.3). The entry accurately restates both required points; no caution is needed.

a_factual: Matches 3.1.A.1 (K = ½mv² is not restated in the body, but nothing in the body contradicts it). 3.1.A.2 says "Translational kinetic energy is a scalar quantity." 3.1.A.3 says "Different observers may measure different values of the translational kinetic energy of an object, depending on the observer's frame of reference." The body and title are faithful paraphrases of these two statements. b_topic_codes: Topic 3.1 (Translational Kinetic Energy) is the first and only place in Unit 3 where translational KE is defined, so owner 3.1 is correct and topic_codes [3.1] is correct. c_ced_required: 3.1.A.2 and 3.1.A.3 are essential knowledge under LO 3.1.A ("Describe the translational kinetic energy of an object in terms of the object's mass and velocity"), so the CED requires students to know them. d_caution: The entry wording is a paraphrase, but the point-earning content (scalar; observers in different frames may measure different values) is stated essentially the same way, so no caution is needed. The ced_evidence quote is an accurate excerpt of 3.1.A.3. No hooks are present.

The entry accurately represents the formula for translational kinetic energy as defined in EK 3.1.A.1. The topic codes are appropriate as kinetic energy is introduced in Topic 3.1, and is directly applied in Topic 3.2 (Work-Energy Theorem) and Topic 3.4 (Conservation of Energy). The caution addresses a highly common student mathematical error regarding the difference between the change in the square of velocity and the square of the change in velocity.

CED 3.1.A.1 gives K = ½mv². Topic 3.1 first requires it; 3.2.A.4 uses changes in kinetic energy in the work–energy theorem, and 3.4.B.1 includes kinetic energy in mechanical energy. The caution correctly distinguishes ½m(v_f² − v_i²) from ½m(Δv)².

a_factual: The body K = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^{2} matches the CED equation in 3.1.A.1 verbatim: "An object's translational kinetic energy is given by the equation K = 1/2 mv^2". Symbols K, m, v are correct and no list is involved. b_topic_codes: owner 3.1 is the first topic that requires the formula (3.1.A.1). Topic 3.2 uses it through the work-energy theorem (3.2.A.4, change in kinetic energy equals net work), and 3.4 uses it through mechanical energy as the sum of kinetic and potential energies (3.4.B.1). Both listed topics use it. c_ced_required: LO 3.1.A reads "Describe the translational kinetic energy of an object in terms of the object's mass and velocity," so students must reproduce and apply this equation. d_caution: The entry's body wording is the CED's wording, so no caution is strictly required. The caution (\Delta K=\tfrac12 m(v_f^2-v_i^2), not \tfrac12 m(\Delta v)^2) is mathematically correct, does not contradict the CED, and flags a real misconception, so it is acceptable. The CED does not state the delta form itself, which is noted but does not fail the check.

The entry accurately reflects the CED statements in Topic 3.2. Specifically, 3.2.A.2 states 'Work is a scalar quantity that may be positive, negative, or zero' and 3.2.A.3.ii states 'The component of the force exerted on a system perpendicular to the direction of the displacement of the system’s center of mass can change the direction of the system’s motion without changing the system’s kinetic energy.'

The scalar-and-sign statement matches 3.2.A.2. But 3.2.A.3.ii says a perpendicular force component “can change” the direction of motion, not that it always changes it, and specifies displacement of the system’s center of mass. For work that changes total energy, 3.2.A.3.i specifies displacement of the force’s point of application. The entry omits those distinctions and has no caution addressing the misleading wording. Topic 3.2 requires these work concepts; 3.4.C.2–3 addresses work and energy transfer.

CED 3.2.A.2 supports the signed-scalar statement, and 3.2.A.3.i supports the title when the displacement is that of the force’s point of application. But 3.2.A.3.ii says a perpendicular component ‘can change the direction’ of motion, not that it necessarily changes it; it also specifies displacement of the system’s center of mass. The entry omits those qualifications and has no caution. Topic 3.2 first requires these work concepts; 3.4.C.2–3 uses work to describe conservation and energy transfer.

The formula for work done by a constant force, $W = F_{\parallel}d = Fd\cos\theta$, is factual and directly required by Topic 3.2 (specifically EK 3.2.A.3 and 3.2.A.3.i, which references the 'Relevant equation' for the parallel component of force and displacement). It is also relevant to Topic 3.5 (Power), where work is used to calculate average power ($P = W/t$).

The formula gives work by a constant force as its signed component along the displacement times that displacement; θ is the angle between the force and displacement. Topic 3.2.A.3 states that work by a constant force is related to the force components and displacement of its point of application, and 3.2.A.3.i specifies the parallel component. Topic 3.5.A.3 uses work to calculate average power, supporting 3.5 as an additional topic code. No caution is needed.

a_factual: W = F_∥d = Fd cosθ is the standard work-by-constant-force relation and matches the CED's description in 3.2.A.3 (work 'related to the components of that force and the displacement') and 3.2.A.3.i (only the component parallel to displacement changes the system's total energy). The CED 'Relevant equation' images for 3.2.A.3.i are not legible in the extracted text, so the symbolic form is verified against physics rather than the CED image. b_topic_codes: 3.2 is the owner, since 3.2.A.3 introduces this relation. 3.5 is a valid secondary code because 3.5.A.4 uses the parallel component of a constant force for instantaneous power, and 3.5.A.3 builds average power from work. c_ced_required: 3.2.A.3 and 3.2.A.3.i require students to relate work to the force component parallel to displacement and the displacement, so applying the relation is required. d_caution: the CED phrases the point as a parallel component times displacement. The body gives that form explicitly and the cosθ form is its equivalent, so no caution is needed to earn the point. Caution is null and correct.

The entry accurately represents the work-energy theorem as described in Essential Knowledge 3.2.A.4 of the AP Physics 1 CED. The caution correctly addresses a very common student mathematical error regarding the change in kinetic energy.

The work–energy theorem and the caution are correct: CED 3.2.A.4 says the change in kinetic energy equals the net work, and 3.1.A.1 gives K = ½mv². But the unqualified expression ΣᵢF∥,ᵢd assumes every force is constant and acts through the same displacement. CED 3.2.A.3 limits the constant-force relationship to the displacement of each force’s point of application; 3.2.A.4.ii specifies when a system may instead be modeled as an object.

Topic 3.2 requires the work-energy theorem: 3.2.A.4 states that the change in kinetic energy equals the sum of the work done by all forces. But the unrestricted equality to ΣᵢF∥,ᵢd is not generally valid. CED 3.2.A.3 specifies a constant force and the displacement of the point where that force is exerted; 3.2.A.5 also describes work as area under a force–displacement graph. The formula needs conditions such as constant force components and the applicable displacement for each force. The caution correctly distinguishes the change in v² from (Δv)².

The entry accurately reflects the CED's definition of work in 3.2.A.1 ('Work is the amount of energy transferred into or out of a system...') and 3.2.A.2 ('Work is a scalar quantity that may be positive, negative, or zero.'). The topic codes are correct as Topic 3.2 introduces work and Topic 3.4 deals with conservation of energy and energy transfer.

The title and body incorrectly make work positive simply because it is done on the system. A force can do negative work on a system: the CED says work may be “positive, negative, or zero” (3.2.A.2) and relates work to the force component parallel to displacement (3.2.A.3.i). Nor does negative work necessarily mean energy leaves the system; internal nonconservative interactions can dissipate mechanical energy (3.4.C.2 and its boundary statement). Topics 3.2 and 3.4 are relevant, with work first required in 3.2, but the stated convention is not required by the CED. No caution addresses the misleading wording.

The energy-transfer direction is correct, and Topics 3.2 and 3.4 address work and energy transfer. But “positive work is work done on the system” incorrectly suggests that negative work cannot also be done on a system. The CED says, “Work is a scalar quantity that may be positive, negative, or zero” (3.2.A.2), and describes work done on a system by a force (3.2.A.1). The cited 3.2.A.1 line alone does not establish the proposed sign convention. With no caution or qualification, the misleading wording remains.

The definition of a conservative force is highly accurate and directly derived from the CED essential knowledge statements 3.2.A.1.i and 3.2.A.1.ii. Topic 3.2 first defines the concept: 3.2.A.1.i says work by a conservative force is “path-independent” and depends only on the system’s “initial and final configurations”; 3.2.A.1.ii says that work is zero if the system returns to its initial configuration. Topics 3.3 and 3.4 also use conservative forces in 3.3.A.1 and 3.4.C.2. The entry closely follows the CED wording, so no caution is needed.

a_factual: The body matches the CED's properties of conservative work. 3.2.A.1.i says the work done by a conservative force is path-independent and depends only on the initial and final configurations; 3.2.A.1.ii says it is zero (or the potential-energy change is zero) when the system returns to its initial configuration. The body's grammar is loose: 'does work that is path-independent' attributes path-independence to the force rather than to the work, and 'is zero if...' has an ambiguous subject.
